name: Brazil under Tite, 2019 Copa America to 2022 World Cup
scopeNote: Counted: all competitive matches from the 2019 Copa America opener (Brazil v Bolivia, 14 June 2019; date from the ESPN reference list in the Wikipedia Copa America page) through the 2022 World Cup quarter-final loss to Croatia (9 December 2022; FIFA/BBC references and FourFourTwo). In between: the 2019 Copa America (title), 2022 World Cup qualifying (started October 2020, unbeaten, 14W-3D-0L per a search summary, and 'undefeated, conceding just five goals and scoring 40 during seventeen matches' per Football Faithful), the 2021 Copa America (final lost to Argentina) and the 2022 World Cup. Matches between July 2018 and June 2019 were NOT counted: they were friendlies only (the Copa America is the first competitive tournament after Russia 2018), and the brief makes friendlies context only. Friendlies inside the period (e.g. Ghana, September 2022) are used only as context. Style terms used by sources: 'tactical flexibility', '4-1-4-1' with Casemiro as deepest midfielder (2019, Coaches' Voice), '4-3-3 or 4-2-3-1' with a 3-2-5 in possession and a 4-4-2 mid-block with counter-press (2022, Football Faithful), 'three consolidated ways of playing' (Sky Sports, Oct 2022). WHAT IS DISTINCT (evidence): (1) wingers: in 2019 the wide attackers were Neymar (injured, ruled out) / Gabriel Jesus / Everton with Firmino as mobile central striker and Coutinho/Arthur inside; from late 2021 Raphinha and Vinicius Jr became two natural, touchline-hugging wingers, making the team 'very direct' with Neymar floating as false nine and Paqueta as the advanced midfielder; (2) full-backs: 2019 Dani Alves moved inside like a midfielder and the left-back went box-to-box; in 2022 full-backs are 'not auxiliary wingers', the right-back tucks in as an extra midfielder (Danilo/Sandro, 'not world-class players'); (3) midfield: 2019 Casemiro + Arthur/Coutinho, Fernandinho; 2022 Casemiro with Fred (drifts left) and Paqueta (offensive, half-spaces), Casemiro drops between centre-backs in a 3-2-5; (4) centre forward: Firmino 2019, Richarlison/Gabriel Jesus 2022 (Firmino left out of the 26); (5) age/personnel: Dani Alves 37 and an old-guard core in 2019, versus Thiago Silva aged 38 but a Vinicius/Raphinha/Rodrygo/Antony/Martinelli wave in 2022, and a record 26 players used at the World Cup; (6) stated view: Tite says young players are chosen by 'the best moment, the degree of confidence' and (March 2022) 'Particularmente, nao gosto de usar falso 9' about Neymar. WHERE THIN: no tier A analysis of 2022 pressing or marking (the ESPN 'were Tite tactics to blame' piece, a Coaches' Voice 2022 piece and several tactical blogs were unreadable or returned security checks); no source found that states zonal vs man marking for this period (Coaches' Voice 2020 says Tite in general, at club level, was among the first in Brazil to use zonal marking, only via search summary and not verified here); nothing verified on set pieces, open training, Alisson/Fabinho roles or Alex Sandro/Danilo usage beyond the Sky Sports quote; the 2019 tactical blog analyses (betweentheposts, footballbh) were not readable, so 2019 shape rests on Coaches' Voice (May 2020, retrospective of the period) and Tite's own Coaches' Voice account of the final. Fred and Paqueta evidence is preview-based (Football Faithful, 15 Nov 2022), not match data. The 2016-18 comparison was not researched beyond the Coaches' Voice paragraphs that describe the 4-1-4-1 and the Alves/Willian/Paulinho/Renato Augusto side of 2017-18.
openQuestions: Which exact competitive match count and date for the first match: 14 June 2019 (Brazil v Bolivia) is taken from Wikipedia's ESPN reference list, not from a match report.
Search summaries claim Dani Alves was 39 and the oldest in the 2022 squad and that Firmino was left out; not verified in a read page (Wikipedia squad table only gives Thiago Silva aged 38).
Did Tite keep zonal marking in 2019-22? Only a general club-level statement was seen in a search summary (Coaches' Voice ES, Flamengo 2023 page), not read.

Coaches' Voice 2020 profile says Alves moved inside in build-up and relied on a 4-1-4-1; confirm with match-level data whether 2021-22 used a 4-2-3-1 or 4-3-3 more often (Football Faithful says both).
Depor quotes Tite's Coaches' Voice interview; the original Coaches' Voice page was not found, so the Peru-final quote is attributed secondhand.

sources.title: Coach Watch: Tite - Coaches' Voice

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: Tite, who has managed the side since 2016 and led them to Copa America success in 2019, tends to be flexible with personnel but tends to favour some variant of a 4-3-3 or 4-2-3-1.

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: Usually, they use a 3-2-5 shape in possession with Casemiro dropping in between the centre-backs and Paqueta and Fred sitting ahead of him.

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: They have also utilised a diamond build-up, with one centre-back pushing high and wide on the right with the left-back tucking in. Marquinhos and Casemiro form the base and tip of the diamond respectively.

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: Brazil tend to dominate possession in most games, methodically working the ball until a quick burst of movement and interchange can create a chance.

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: in Vinicius Junior and Raphinha, Brazil possess two hard-working, natural wingers who love hugging the touchline.

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: Defensively, Brazil fall into a 4-4-2 mid-block but counter-press aggressively in central areas. Led by either Richarlison or Jesus, both of whom are excellent pressers

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: Even in deeper areas of the pitch, Brazil keep a compact yet aggressive defensive structure.

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: Tite wants his team to seek counter-attacking opportunities whenever possible, resulting in a defensive strategy that aims to retrieve possession as quickly as possible rather than ceding the ball for the sake of solidity itself.

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: Paqueta, another nominal central midfielder, has a much more offensive role. He drives forward with the ball, makes runs into the box to pose as a late-arriving goal threat, and spends lots of time in the half spaces as a creative focal point.

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: In midfield, Fred often drifts to the left wide space to provide defensive cover for the fullback and winger on that flank.

sources.title: World Cup Preview: How Tite's flexible setup makes Brazil dangerous (The Football Faithful)
sources.evidence: At times, Brazil can seem bereft of ideas when facing an especially well-drilled defensive block.
